Bring
brĭng
v.t. (to bear or conduct to a place; rendering Hebrew bo in the causative, Greek agō, pherō)
Saxon bringan, to bear along. In Scripture the verb is overwhelmingly God's: He brings out, brings in, brings forth, and brings to pass.

Biblical Definition

To bring is to carry a thing or a person from where they are to where they must be, and in Scripture the great subject of the verb is God. He brought Israel out: “Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt” (Exo 3:10) — and note that Moses is sent, but the bringing is the LORD's work through him. He brings the believer's committed way to its end: “Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass” (Psa 37:5), which is the whole doctrine of providence in a single verb. He brings the dead with Christ: “them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him” (1Th 4:14). And He brings sons home through suffering: “in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings” (Heb 2:10). Salvation, in Hebrews' language, is a bringing — a company of sons conducted to glory behind a Captain who went the road first. Man does not bring himself. He is brought.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines bring as to fetch, to bear from a distant place, to convey or remove to a nearer place, and to procure or cause to come.

expand to see more

BRING, v.t. To fetch; to bear, convey or lead from a distant to a nearer place.

2. To produce; to procure as a cause; to draw to.

3. To attract or draw along.

4. To cause to come; to cause to proceed from a distant place, in company, or at the same time.

To bring to pass, to effect; to accomplish.

Key Scripture

Exo 3:10 — "Come now therefore, and I will send thee unto Pharaoh, that thou mayest bring forth my people the children of Israel out of Egypt."

Psa 37:5 — "Commit thy way unto the LORD; trust also in him; and he shall bring it to pass."

1Th 4:14 — "For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him."

Heb 2:10 — "For it became him, for whom are all things, and by whom are all things, in bringing many sons unto glory, to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings."

Modern Corruption

A generation trained to bring itself — to self-actualise, self-deliver, self-make — has no grammar left for a salvation in which the sinner is the object of the verb and God its subject.

expand to see more

The plainest evidence of a doctrine is who governs the verbs, and modern religion has quietly changed the subject. God's part becomes offering, enabling, or accompanying; man's part becomes the actual bringing. But Hebrews says the Father is bringing many sons unto glory, Psalm 37 says He shall bring it to pass, and Exodus says He brought Israel out with a stretched-out arm. Where the verb is handed back to man, assurance goes with it, because a soul that brought itself this far must now bring itself the rest of the way.

The pastoral consequence is exhaustion. Committing a way to the LORD and trusting Him to bring it to pass is rest; managing outcomes on His behalf is not. And the promise is not that God brings the believer round the sufferings — Hebrews 2:10 says the Captain Himself was made perfect through them, which means the road to glory runs through the very trouble the believer keeps asking to be brought around. He brings sons home; He does not always bring them the way they would have chosen.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bo (H935) in the causative, to cause to come or bring in; Greek agō (G71), to lead, and pherō (G5342), to bear — the verbs of exodus and of glory.

expand to see more

Hebrew bo (H935) — to come or go; in the hiphil, to bring in, bring out, bring to pass; the standard verb of the exodus (Exo 3:8).

Hebrew yatsa (H3318) — in the hiphil, to bring forth, lead out; “I brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians” (Exo 6:7).

Greek agō (G71) — to lead or bring; Hebrews' “bringing many sons unto glory” (Heb 2:10).

Usage

"“He shall bring it to pass” — providence stated as a promise to the committed way."

"“Bringing many sons unto glory” — salvation as a conducted journey behind a Captain."

"“Them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him” — the grave does not lose the escort."
